doc.title: Adaptive Script, ECMAScript, and TypeScript
doc.paragraph: Adaptive Script's syntax is close to ECMAScript's and TypeScript's, and many of its built-in functions have the names of ECMAScript methods, so if you know either one you can read most scripts right away. It is a language of its own, though, compiled and run by Adaptive Framework, and the rest of this reference describes it on its own terms. This page collects the places where the two differ, so that coming from ECMAScript or TypeScript holds no surprises. The biggest differences come first; after them, the details are grouped by topic.

section.title: The Big Differences
section.paragraph: If you read only one part of this page, read this one. These are the differences you are most likely to meet in your first script:

row.column: "a" + 1 is "a1"; 1 == "1" is true; Number(s) converts anything
A value is never converted unless you ask. "a" + 1, 1 + 1.0, and 1 == 1.0 are errors. Write "a" + to_string(1) or to_double(1) + 1.0.
Any value is truthy or falsy: if (count), !name, a || "default"
if, while, ?:, !, &&, and || take a boolean. Write if (count > 0), a ?? "default", or boolean(v) for truthiness.
integer (64 bits, exact) and double are separate data types. 7 / 2 is 3.
TypeScript checks types when compiling, then erases them
A data type you write on a let, parameter, or return is checked every time the script runs, and v as T checks too.
Dates, URLs, and so on are strings or objects
Dates, times, durations, URIs, email addresses, and more are data types of their own, written as typed literals: "2026-10-11"date, "https://example.com/"uri.
a.map(f) on a prototype; classes, this, new
Functions take the value first: map(a, f), or a->map(f). There are no classes, prototypes, this, or new.
function (x) { return x + 1; }; there are no arrow functions.
=== on objects and arrays compares identity
Unicode code points, always NFC: an emoji has length 1.
Semicolons may be left out; any expression can be a statement
Every statement ends with ;, and an expression on its own is not a statement.
throw any value; catch gets that value
throw takes a message, optional data, and an optional id; catch gets an error object.
Qualified variables such as current::object and request::; there are no globals or modules.

list.item: var: declare with let or const.

Classes, prototypes, new, super, delete, and this. Built-in types such as Array, Object, String, Map, and Error are not there; their methods are functions (see Functions named after ECMAScript methods below).
Arrow functions. => appears only in function types.
The in operator: use property_exists(o, name).
for .. in: walk keys, values, or entries with for .. of.
typeof and instanceof: use is_T(v), such as is_integer(v). The words are reserved so a script copied from elsewhere fails right away.
The arguments object: declare a rest parameter, ...rest.
Generators, user-defined iterators, and asynchronous operations (async, await, Promises).
Importing modules: share code through qualified variables.
eval of a string: hold the source in a script value and run it with eval(script(s)). The code can not see or change variables outside it, and evaluate("1 + 1") is just the string.

to_T(s) reads text strictly with data type T's parser: to_integer(" 12") and to_integer("1.5") are errors, where Number(" 12") is 12. Number text is read as XML Schema writes it, so to_double("5") is 5.0.
There are no conversion functions named after a data type, like Number(x) or String(x); integer(x) and dateTime(s) are compile errors that name the typed literal or to_T to use.
boolean(v) is Boolean(v) truthiness, so boolean("false") is true. string_to_boolean(s) reads boolean text.

A typed literal, "2026-10-11T12:00:00Z"dateTime, has no ECMAScript equivalent. The closest, a tagged template, runs a function when the script runs; a typed literal is read when the script is compiled.
A template string that is a single substitution, `${v}`, is v itself, whatever its data type: `${[1, 2]}` is an array. A template literal in ECMAScript is always a string.
null and undefined are both nullish, and null is a data type of its own.
integer and double do not mix: 1 + 1.0 is an error; write to_double(1) + 1.0. An integer divided by zero, or an integer result that does not fit in 64 bits, is an error.
Integer ** is exact; a negative exponent or a result too large for an integer is an error.

Doubles follow IEEE 754's default handling, as ECMAScript's numbers do: 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity, 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN, and a comparison with NaN is false. #compile strictDouble; makes invalid operations and division by zero errors instead, the way a C compiler option can; ECMAScript has no way to ask for that.
As in ECMAScript, -2 ** 2 is a syntax error; write (-2) ** 2 or -(2 ** 2).

The math functions (sqrt, sin, log, hypot, ...) are ECMAScript's Math functions, but take a double only (sqrt(4) says to write to_double(v)), and hypot needs at least one value (ECMAScript's Math.hypot() is 0). round rounds halves toward positive infinity, as Math.round does.

The compiler literals #pi, #e, #ln2, #ln10, #log2e, #log10e, #sqrt2, and #sqrt1_2 are the Math constants. #doubleMin is the smallest normal double; ECMAScript's Number.MIN_VALUE is the smallest subnormal one, #doubleMinSubnormal. #integerMaxExactDouble is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, the largest integer a JavaScript client reading the JSON keeps exactly.
.5, 1., and 1.e10 are double literals, as in ECMAScript; a number with no . or exponent is an integer.

A string is Unicode code points, not UTF-16 code units: length, indexes, at, slice, substring, code_point_at, and the padding functions all count code points, so an emoji is one, never two halves. "😀" has length 1, and half of a surrogate pair on its own is an error.

Every string is NFC normalized, so equal text is always equal: a decomposed e and combining acute accent is the same string as a precomposed é, wherever either came from. normalize takes "NFC" and "NFKC"; "NFD" and "NFKD" are errors, since the result could not be a string. ECMAScript strings are not normalized.
A string never holds U+FEFF (the byte order mark): it is dropped wherever it appears. ECMAScript keeps it as a character.
+ does not convert: "a" + 1 is an error; write "a" + to_string(1), concat("a", 1), or `a${1}`.

map, filter, and the other array walkers take an array only, so write [...s]->map(f) for the characters of a string. Functions named after String methods, such as slice and at, keep their string meaning.
An empty search string in replace matches between code points, not UTF-16 code units: replace("abc", "", "x", -1) is "xaxbxcx", as replaceAll would give.
pad_start and pad_end with an empty fill string, when padding is needed, are an error; ECMAScript returns the value unpadded.
trim, to_upper_case, and to_lower_case use ECMAScript's white space and Unicode full case mapping, the same in every locale.
url_encode and url_decode are encodeURI and decodeURI.
A semicolon ends every statement; it is never inserted for you.
An expression on its own is not a statement ('abc'; and x + 1; are errors); a call, an assignment, ++, and -- are statements.
Assignment is a statement, not an expression: x = y = 1; works, but if ((x = next()) > 0) and let x = y = 1 do not. Writing = for === is then always caught.
A let read before it is assigned is undefined, not a ReferenceError.
A let or const as the unbraced body of an if or a loop is a syntax error. Labels go on loops only, not on blocks or if.

throw takes a message string, then optional data and id clauses. The id is one of those a request can answer with (not_found, denied, ...). catch always receives an error object with message, data, id, and errorCode, not the thrown value, and throw; in a catch throws it again.
switch is ECMAScript's, plus an optional using function to compare a value with each case.
A function declared : void is a procedure: its call is the void value, not undefined, so it does not change the script's result. ECMAScript has no such return type.
Closures capture let and const bindings and parameters, as in ECMAScript.
===, includes, index_of, and last_index_of compare by value, so an equal array or object is found; ECMAScript compares objects by identity. index_of finds NaN, as includes does in ECMAScript.
Arrays have no holes: an omitted value in an array literal is an undefined entry, and create_array(n, v) is new Array(n).fill(v).

Arrays have no properties, only entries. a[i] counts from the start only, as in ECMAScript: a[-1] is undefined, at(a, -1) is the last entry, and a[-1] = v is an error, where ECMAScript adds a property named "-1".
push and unshift return the new length, as in ECMAScript.
concat of arrays takes only arrays; write [...a, v] or push(a, v) to add one value.
sort with no compare function orders values as < does, so [10, 9, 1] sorts to [1, 9, 10]; ECMAScript compares them as strings. A compare function may also return a boolean.

A script function passed to map, filter, reduce, and the like is called with (value, index, array), as in ECMAScript; a built-in function is called with the value alone, so map(a, to_string) works, where ["1", "2"].map(parseInt) famously does not.
Object property names are strings; a number or boolean in brackets is an error, not converted. from_entries and group_by want string names too.
An array can be typed, array<integer>(1, 2), and then holds only integers. ECMAScript's typed arrays hold only numbers of one size.

section.title: TypeScript Types
section.paragraph: Type annotations are spelled as in TypeScript, but they are a smaller language, and they mean more when the script runs.

list.item: A data type on a let, parameter, or return is checked whenever the script runs, even with type checking off, and is never converted: n(1.9) for a parameter x: integer is an error. TypeScript's types are gone by then. Object shapes, tuples, and function types are checked at run time when type checking is on.

v as T checks: it returns v if it is a T and is an error if not, where TypeScript's only tells the compiler. It never converts, null as string is an error, and v as T + 1 needs parentheses, (v as T) + 1. For now T is a data type.
The types are Adaptive data types (integer, string, dateTime, ...), not number, and there are no literal types such as "read" or 1.
An array type is T[] only; there is no Array<T>.
A tuple has a fixed length: no optional, rest, or labeled elements.
An object type lists its properties, with ? for optional ones. There are no index signatures, method signatures (write run: (a: integer) => boolean), readonly, or declaration merging.
A type or interface name must be declared before it is used, like let, except that a type may refer to itself.

Not in Adaptive Script: generics, keyof, conditional and mapped types, enum, never, satisfies, type predicates, assertion functions, the non-null !, implements, type queries with typeof, and type-only imports.
Type checking at compile time is turned on per environment or per script (#compile typeCheck;), not by a separate tool such as tsc.

section.title: Regular Expressions
section.paragraph: Regular expressions are ICU's, whose syntax follows the Perl tradition that Python and Java also come from. ECMAScript keeps some rules for compatibility with its first, ASCII and UTF-16 days, so these give a different answer than ECMAScript, most of them the same answer as Perl and Python:

list.item: \d, \w, and \b are Unicode, as in Perl and Python 3: é is a word character and ٣ is a digit. For ASCII only, write [0-9] or [A-Za-z0-9_].
The i flag uses full Unicode case folding, as Perl does: /strasse/i matches "Straße".

Without the m flag, $ also matches just before a line terminator at the end of the value, as in Perl, Python, and Java: test(/^ab$/, "ab\n") is true. Write \z for the very end (and \Z for the end or just before a final line terminator, as in Perl and Java).
The line terminators are LF, CR, CR LF, U+0085, U+2028, and U+2029, so . does not match U+0085.
[^] is a syntax error. Write [\s\S], or use the s flag.
A lookbehind must have a bounded length.

A string search in split and replace is literal text, and so is its replacement; only a regexp search reads groups in the replacement. Write $0 for the whole match (ECMAScript $&), ${name} for a named group ($<name>), and \$ for a dollar sign ($$).
There are no g, y, d, or v flags. Use match_all, or the limit of replace, for every match.
ICU also has things ECMAScript does not, such as \A, \z, \Z, the x flag, inline flags (?i), atomic groups (?>...), and possessive quantifiers a*+.

section.title: Functions Named After ECMAScript Methods
section.paragraph: A function takes what ECMAScript calls the receiver as its first parameter, and x->f(a) calls f(x, a), so a->map(fn) reads as ECMAScript's a.map(fn). The arrow is the same idea as Perl's $x->f($a). It is not ., because . reads a property: if it also found built-in functions, a property with the name of a function would hide it, depending on the data. Names are snake case. Some that differ more than that:

row.column: a.with(i, v) (with is a reserved word)
s.match(re) without the g flag, s.matchAll(re)
s.replace; a limit of -1 is s.replaceAll

section.paragraph: A match is an _AdaptiveRegexpMatch_ object, since an Adaptive array has no properties: its captures[n] is m[n] of ECMAScript's match array, its index counts code points, and its groups is m.groups. A replacement function is called with that object, instead of ECMAScript's list of groups, and must return a string.

row.column: "2026-10-11T12:00:00Z"dateTime, or to_dateTime(s) for text from elsewhere
x as dateTime, checked when the script runs
